Gamepad joysticks and mouse controls are both analog

Actually mice are digital, it's just that the sample size for laser reads is high enough that you can't tell. Analog mice (remember when mice had balls?) haven't been sold in a very long time now.

If you graph an analog signal, it will have peaks and troughs comprised of curves. If you graph a digital signal you'll get something similar, but the curve will be comprised of steps. How good digital is depends on how small those steps can be made. This is often measured in DPI (dots per inch, sometimes also called PPI or pulses per inch) in mice. DPI measures the number of samples a mouse can make when moved one inch in any direction. In mice, the steps are so small (some gaming mice get up over 1600 DPI) it no longer matters.

A joystick is analog when it depends on a device called a potentiometer. This is what makes an axis of an analog joystick work. Inside a potentiometer you find a conductive track with a contact that can slide along the track changing the distance current needs to travel. When the track is made long, it has more resistance than when the track is made short. When a current is passed through it the result is measurable. Because the distance between two points is infinitely divisible, you get a smoother curve with more potential points. In digital, each point in the scale is fixed and not divisible.

I was more referring to the fact that when you move a mouse a tiny bit, your character will move only a tiny bit and stop. If you move that same joystick a tiny bit, the character will start moving and not stop until you let go of the joystick. Mouse = analog; move the mouse and the input only moves as far. Joystick = digital; the controls are either on or off, move a bit and it keeps moving until you let it go and turn the digital on/off switch back to off.

Your use of terms is not correct. The terms "analog" and "digital" have nothing to do with most joysticks having springs that cause them to return to center. It only has to do with how the signal is formed. All modern mice are digital. Most (with some exceptions) modern joysticks are analog.

When you move a mouse, the motion is translated to the computer analogously, hence the term "analog". When you move a joystick, its motion is relative. Please feel free to use whatever terms you like to describe this difference. But the long and short of it is this: analogous controls for the win. I've played both and I know that I could very easily beat myself using mouse/keyboard over a joystick. That's the point I was attempting to make.

Except that's not what analog means. The problem here isn't your analysis of how the devices act, it's that you're applying terms to them that don't make sense. You need to spend a minute to learn what "analog" and "digital" actually means in terms of electronics. The terms you're actually looking for are absolute vs relative positioning. Joysticks use absolute positioning while mice use relative positioning. This is to say that a joystick will give the same positional value if it is moved to the same place every time. A joystick reports a series of changing absolute positions until it stops moving. A mouse on the other hand can be moved around on it's surface, so it is relative to whatever its starting position is. A mouse does not report a position, it reports a direction and speed of movement.

Also, the translation of mouse and joystick movements are almost never a straight ramp. Most people use some form of acceleration in order to have a ramp that curves over distance allowing you to cover more screen area using a smaller amount of physical space or movement depending on the distance and speed of the movement.
A joystick is considered analog by any reasonable standard and person

Yes and no, it depends on the kind of joystick. For example, Microsoft used to make a joystick called a "Sidewinder Precision Pro" that operated not with potentiometers, but with a laser that changed positions with joystick movement and was read much like a mouse is. So in reality, whether a joystick is analog or not depends on what technology is driving its operation. OTOH, digital joysticks that act similar to analog joysticks are a lot less common because they're more expensive to make well and they're not necessarily better than potentiometer driven sticks. The most commonly recognizable digital joystick is the D-Pad, a modern refinement of early joysticks dating all the way back to the Atari 2600 joystick which was also a D-Pad in that it only had 4 contacts, giving a total of 8 possible digital directions.
